record.tranche_reason: The study compares SAE reconstruction errors and downstream loss after replacing baseline SAEs with rational-activation SAEs. It does not use the original study's dark-matter predictability or cross-size error measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports synthetic rational-activation fitting and sparse-probing results; these do not measure the claim versions. Its downstream loss results have no equal-size random-error comparison.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It proposes a rational-activation SAE and compares it with released ReLU, JumpReLU and TopK SAEs on MSE, ℓ0, alive fraction, ΔCE and loss recovered. It never analyses the SAE error vector: no linear predictability of the error, no cross-size error scaling, no random-error control, no split into linear and nonlinear error, and no circuit or steering use of the error term. It does not cite the dark-matter paper. It mentions known SAE pathologies (shrinkage, dead latents) only as motivation. The reconstruction gains are its own method's performance against baselines, which the rules exclude as a test. So it neither tests nor uses the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors claim RSAE strictly improves on the teacher SAEs in reconstruction and downstream metrics without hurting sparse-probing accuracy. Their own count is 22/24 reconstruction cells and 13/16 downstream cells, not uniform. Pythia ReLU ΔCE is worse (0.259→0.279) and Gemma TopK ΔCE is tied (0.093).
record.recipe_differences: The paper introduces a rational-activation SAE initialized from pretrained SAEs and then fine-tuned; it does not apply the original study's SAE-error predictability or cross-size error analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that results vary by host model and baseline activation family; the ReLU/Pythia-160m downstream cross-entropy result is a marginal regression, and the TopK/Gemma-2-2B cross-entropy result is tied, as summarized in §5.2.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing a fixed SAE activation with a trainable rational one and fine-tuning for 2K steps lowers reconstruction MSE versus the teacher SAE. The gain is about 2–11% for most pairs, but about 53% (Gemma JumpReLU) and 88% (Pythia JumpReLU) for weak JumpReLU teachers. ΔCE also improves in 13 of 16 downstream cells.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Part of SAE reconstruction error depends on the encoder activation's functional form and can be reduced by a more flexible activation at similar sparsity.

record.problems: The downstream-loss results have no matched random-error control, so they cannot establish that SAE errors harm loss more than random errors of equal size. Evaluation covers three open-weight models and selected SAE baselines; the paper notes that other frontier models remain unexplored. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the main SAE metrics.

untested.parts: All: no regression of the SAE error on the input activation.
All: no per-token error-norm prediction, cross-size comparison or scaling.
All: no random-error or equal-norm control for the loss degradation.
All: no split into linear and nonlinear error.
All: no circuit or steering analysis with or without the error term.
Whether dark matter (in the predictable or nonlinear sense) shrinks with architecture or training changes; only total reconstruction MSE of a fine-tuned new architecture is reported.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2 / 'tests' classification and its V6 'supports' label are not justified. The paper never measures dark matter, and its MSE gains are its own method's performance, with λ tuned to maximise wins and unmatched ℓ0 in some pairs. The V3 rows lack the required random-error baseline. I treat the study as not testing the claim. The reconstruction gains are recorded under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Whether SAE error vectors are linearly predictable from input activations.
Per-token error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, shared failure contexts, and whether error persists with scale.
The paper measures loss degradation from SAE reconstructions, but does not compare it with random errors of the same size.
Whether linear error corresponds to unlearned features and nonlinear error resists further dictionary learning.
Whether circuit or steering analyses lose behavior when SAE error is omitted.

The study tests whether a different SAE activation architecture can reduce reconstruction MSE, but does not establish whether dark matter is mostly a training artifact, test the listed training mechanisms individually, or compare with end-to-end training.

relation.reason: It discusses reconstruction fidelity, shrinkage and dead latents as SAE limitations, without testing the claim versions or using dark matter as a tool.

tranche.reason: The study benchmarks its own SAE method without testing error predictability, scaling, equal-norm random-error controls, error decomposition, or functional contributions of retained error. Reconstruction improvements alone do not establish V6's attribution of dark matter mostly to training artifacts.

source_check.notes: Appendix B.1 says Tables 1–2 select λ to maximize strict metric wins, limiting interpretation of the method comparisons. The pack's authors_conclusion repeats a source prose error: Table 2 places the Gemma ΔCE tie at 0.093 under JumpReLU; TopK changes from 0.136 to 0.092.

reader_labels.condition: RSAE versus the listed baseline SAE families on GPT-2 small, Pythia-160m, and Gemma-2-2B
reader_labels.reason: Reconstruction MSE is lower for the fine-tuned RSAE in each reported model/baseline pair; this supports the architecture-related part of V6 but does not establish that dark matter is mostly a training artifact (r17–r24).
